title: Braniff 250
summary: Braniff Flight 250, a BAC 1-11-203AE with 42 persons aboard (4 crew, 38 passengers), broke up in flight at 2312 CST on August 6, 1966 near Falls City, Nebraska. The aircraft encountered extreme turbulence in a roll cloud approximately 5 miles from the nearest radar weather echo while operating in an area of avoidable hazardous weather. The turbulence, caused by wind shears from an approaching squall line, was probably a large-angled gust of very short duration with components in the lateral, vertical, and longitudinal planes. The fin and right tailplane reached their ultimate loads with near-simultaneous failure (p. 62). The right wing subsequently failed. The aircraft tumbled in a random motion, stabilizing into a flat spin before impacting terrain, destroying the aircraft completely.
probable_cause: The Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was inflight structural failure caused by extreme turbulence during operation of the aircraft in an area of avoidable hazardous weather.

factors.evidence: Aircraft encountered severe squall line oriented across flight route with active thunderstorms and strong wind shears (p. 8-9). Weather Bureau forecast called for isolated severe thunderstorms with hail and wind gusts to 65-70 knots (p. 72). Sigmet Bravo 2 at 1920 and Sigmet Bravo 3 at 2215 called for thunderstorm lines with tops at 35,000-46,000 feet (p. 72). Weather was adequately forecast and reported; company forecast was somewhat inaccurate on intensity (p. 61).

Extreme turbulence produced forces and accelerations causing fin and right tailplane to reach ultimate loads with near-simultaneous failures (p. 62). Aircraft then pitched downward until right wing reached its negative ultimate load (p. 62). Loss of these components rendered aircraft uncontrollable (p. 62).

Extreme turbulence was probably a large-angled gust of very short duration with components in lateral, vertical, and longitudinal planes generated by strong horizontal and vertical wind shears associated with outflow of cold air from approaching squall line (p. 62).

Aircraft broke up in roll cloud approximately 5 miles from nearest radar weather echo (p. 62). Aircraft then probably began random tumbling motion which stabilized into flat-spinning attitude before impact 7.6 statute miles on bearing 024.5 degrees from Falls City at elevation 1,078 feet MSL (p. 9).

events.text: Braniff Flight 250 departed New Orleans for Minneapolis with intermediate stops at Shreveport, Fort Smith, Tulsa, Kansas City, and Omaha
Flight departed Kansas City on IFR clearance to Omaha via Jet Route 41 at FL 200; initially restricted to 5,000 feet due to conflicting traffic (p. 7)
Kansas City ARTCC initiated transfer of control to Chicago ARTCC; flight requested and received permission to deviate left of course (p. 8)
Kansas City controller cleared flight to descend to and maintain 5,000 feet and contact Chicago ARTCC (p. 8)

After discussion of weather on Chicago controller's radar, crew of other Braniff flight (255) climbing to 17,000 feet reported light to moderate chop 15 miles southeast of Omaha and expected to be out of it in 10 miles (p. 8)
Flight 250 terminated conversation with Flight 255 regarding weather; this was last transmission received from Flight 250 (p. 8)

Aircraft encounter extreme turbulence in roll cloud approximately 5 miles from nearest radar weather echo with large-angled gust of very short duration with lateral, vertical, and longitudinal components (p. 62)
Fin and right tailplane reached ultimate loads with near-simultaneous failure causing aircraft to pitch downward (p. 62)
Right wing reached negative ultimate load and failed, rendering aircraft uncontrollable (p. 62)

Aircraft entered random tumbling motion which stabilized into flat-spinning attitude before impact near Falls City, Nebraska, 7.6 statute miles bearing 024.5 degrees from town at elevation 1,078 feet MSL, destroying aircraft completely (p. 9, 62)

Ground witnesses observed explosion in sky followed by fireball falling from clouds (p. 9). Wind shift from south to north observed after accident with velocity 30-60 mph and light to moderate rain in accident area (p. 9)
